figures.caption: FIG. 1. Adaptation strength and random connectivity organize distinct dynamical regimes. The panels show individual neuron time traces xi(t) across dynamical regimes. Rows correspond to increasing random coupling strength g = 1.2 (below chaos), 1.8, and 2.0 (both above chaos). Columns correspond to increasing adaptation strength β = 0, 0.35, 0.55, 0.85, 1.4. At g = 1.2, the coherent mode loses stability before chaos onset: the network passes directly from static fixed points to global oscillation (Regime IV) at large β. At g = 1.8 and g = 2.0, the network is chaotic and the full sequence of regimes is visible: noise-sustained oscillation (Regime II), irregular switching between wells (Regime III), and global oscillation (Regime IV). Time is shown in units of τm, with τa = 30. Parameters: N = 4000, τa = 30, σm = σn = 2.0, γ = 0.7.

FIG. 2. The coherent mode progresses from local oscillations to switching and global cycles. The panels show phase portraits of the coherent overlap κ(t) and the adaptation overlap κa(t) from network simulations. Top row: g = 1.8; bottom row: g = 2.0. Columns from left to right: β = 0.35, 0.55, 0.85, 1.4. At g = 1.8: regular then irregular noise-sustained oscillation within one basin; global oscillation with lobes around the unstable fixed points; smooth limit cycle. At g = 2.0, stronger chaos advances the sequence: irregular oscillation; switching between basins; limit cycle with dwelling near the basin; smooth relaxation oscillation. Parameters as in Fig. 1.

FIG. 3. Adaptation concentrates fixed points near high gain and lowers the chaos threshold. The panels show the fixed-point membrane-potential distribution p(x∗). Histograms show network simulations at g = 1.8 and N = 4000. Solid curves show the DMFT prediction p(x∗) = ph(F (x∗))F ′(x∗), where ph = N (0,Σ2∗ h ). As the adaptation strength β increases, the adaptation-induced diffeomorphism F (x) = x + β tanh(x) compresses the distribution toward zero. This compression concentrates neurons in the high-gain region, increases the squared-gain susceptibility χ2,x, and thereby lowers the chaos onset threshold gc ∝ 1/ √ χ2,x. Parameters are as in Fig. 1.

FIG. 4. DMFT predicts the coherent fixed-point branch and gain statistics. Top row: γ = 0.7; bottom row: γ = 0.5. Left: overlap magnitude |κ∗| versus β. Center: input variance Σ2∗ h versus β. Right: fourth-moment susceptibility χ∗ 2,x versus β. Solid curves: theory (stable fixed-point branch). Points with error bars: simulations at N = 4000, averaged over 5 random realizations. Different colors correspond to g = 1.0, 1.2, 1.4, 1.6, 1.8. The curves terminate where the fixed point ceases to exist. Parameters: σm = σn = 2.0, τa = 30.

FIG. 5. Adaptation deforms the random bulk toward a resonant instability. The panels show eigenvalue spectra of the linearized dynamics in the complex s-plane. Top row: g = 1.8; bottom row: g = 2.0. Columns correspond to increasing β. Blue dots: numerically computed eigenvalues of the 2N -dimensional Jacobian (N = 4000). Orange dots: eigenvalues with Re(s) > 0 (unstable). Black curves: theoretical spectral boundary from Eq. (30). At β = 0 the boundary is a circle centered at s = −1 with radius g √ χ2,x. As β increases, the boundary develops a resonant bulge near Im(s) ∼ 1/ √ τa and compresses at low frequencies, in quantitative agreement with the mean-field prediction. At large β, eigenvalues cross the imaginary axis preferentially near the resonant frequency. Parameters as in Fig. 1.

FIG. 6. DMFT captures the adaptation-induced resonant peak. The left panel shows the firing-rate power spectral density Sϕ(f) just above the chaos threshold, at approximately g/gc ≈ 1.07. The right panel shows the corresponding autocovariance function Cϕ(τ) for the same parameter values. Colors indicate g = 1.6, 1.8, and 2.0. Solid curves show simulation medians, and shaded bands show interquartile ranges. Dashed curves show the self-consistent spectral DMFT prediction from Sec. VI. The spectral peak near f ≈ 0.02–0.03 reflects the resonant frequency introduced by adaptation. Parameters are as in Fig. 1.

FIG. 7. The resonant peak shifts upward with adaptation strength. Peak frequency fpeak of the fluctuation spectrum versus β for g = 1.6 (red), 1.8 (blue), 2.0 (purple). Box plots: simulation (median, interquartile range, and extremes across neurons). Dashed lines: DMFT prediction. The peak frequency increases with β as the adaptation resonance shifts to higher frequencies. Parameters as in Fig. 1.

FIG. 8. Adaptation increases incoherent firing-rate variance above chaos. Incoherent variance σ2 ϕ of firingrate fluctuations versus β. Box plots: simulation; dashed lines: DMFT theory. Colors as in Fig. 7. The variance increases with β within each g series, reflecting stronger chaotic fluctuations as adaptation modifies the gain distribution. Parameters as in Fig. 1.

FIG. 9. Chaos and coherent Hopf boundaries partition the phase diagram. Phase diagram in the (g, β) plane for γ = 0.7 (left) and γ = 0.5 (right). Solid line: chaos onset gc(β) from Eq. (31). Dashed line: coherent Hopf boundary from Eq. (53). Grey region: static coherent state. Between the two boundaries, the color map shows the incoherent variance σ2 ϕ from the spectral DMFT. This is the noise-sustained oscillation regime, where the coherent mode is a stable focus driven by chaotic fluctuations. The orange segment of the Hopf boundary marks the switching region, where the two boundaries are close and chaotic fluctuations can drive transitions between basins. Blue region: global limit cycle.

FIG. 10. The reduced deterministic model captures the local bifurcation structure. Phase portraits of the reduced deterministic model (55) in the (κ, κa) plane at g = 1.8 for increasing adaptation strength. Green dashed curves: κ̇ = 0 nullcline. Purple dashed lines: κ̇a = 0 nullcline (κa = βκ). Stars: stable fixed points; crosses: unstable fixed points (where applicable). Gray streamlines show the vector field; colored trajectories illustrate representative solutions from different initial conditions. (a) β = 0.35: the fixed points are stable nodes; trajectories converge monotonically. (b) β = 0.55: the fixed points have become stable foci; the spiraling return flow underlies the noise-sustained oscillation of Regime II. (c) β = 0.85: the foci approach the Hopf boundary; the narrowed basins of attraction permit noise-driven switching between wells (Regime III). (d) β = 1.40: the fixed points have lost stability and a global limit cycle encircles both wells (Regime IV). Parameters as in Fig. 1.

FIG. 11. A stochastic reduced model reproduces the regime transitions and the global shape of the limit cycle. Three-dimensional trajectories in (κ, κa,Σ 2 h) space showing the progression of dynamical regimes. Top row: full RNN simulations (N = 4000, g = 1.8). Bottom row: low-dimensional SDE model (59) with DMFT-calibrated parameters. Left column (β = 0.45 for both): noise-sustained oscillation confined to a single well; the trajectory spirals around a stable focus, with the chaotic bulk providing the energy that maintains the oscillation. Middle column (β = 0.75 for the RNN, β = 0.95 for the SDE): irregular switching between the two wells; chaotic fluctuations occasionally kick the trajectory across the separatrix. Right column (β = 1.40 for both): global limit cycle carrying κ between both wells. The reduced SDE model qualitatively reproduces the full sequence of regimes observed in the network simulations. Parameters as in Fig. 1.
